﴿Iram﴾ is the tribe of ʿAd, named after one of their forefathers, just as it is said "Hashim" for the Banu Hashim. Its benefit is that what is meant is the first ʿAd, since the later ʿAd are not called by this name. It has also been said: Iram is the name of their city, so it is on the deletion of a modifier, its estimated meaning being: "by ʿAd of Iram." This is supported by the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr, "bi-ʿAdin Iram," in which ʿAd is an idafa (construct) with its tanwin removed. Iram is not declined on either view, because of definiteness and feminine form. ﴿Dhat al-ʿImad﴾: whoever says Iram is a tribe says that al-ʿImad refers to the pillars of their buildings or the pillars of their houses made of hair, because they were people of pillars. Ibn ʿAbbas said that this is a metaphor for the great height of their bodies. Whoever says Iram is a city says that al-ʿImad refers to the stones with which it was built, and it has been said that it refers to palaces and towers. ﴿Which were not created the like of in the lands﴾ is an attribute of the tribe, because they were the greatest of people in bodily stature; it is said that a man among them had a height of four hundred cubits. Or it is an attribute of the city, and this is more apparent, because of His saying "in the lands," and because it was the most beautiful of the cities of the world. It is related that Shaddad ibn ʿAd built it over three hundred years, and his lifespan was nine hundred years, and he made its palaces of gold and silver, and its pillars of chrysolite and rubies, and in it were varieties of trees and flowing rivers. It is related that he heard mention of Paradise and wished to make something like it. When he completed it and set out toward it with the people of his kingdom, Allah destroyed them with a single cry. This city was in Yemen. It is related that some Muslims passed by it during the caliphate of Muawiya. It has also been said that it is Damascus, and it has been said that it is Alexandria, but this is weak. ﴿Who hewed the rock in the valley﴾: that is, they bored into it and carved houses in it. The wadi is what lies between two mountains, and there was no water in it. It has been said that he meant Wadi al-Qura. ﴿And Pharaoh, lord of the stakes﴾ is mentioned in Surah Sad. ﴿Who transgressed in the lands﴾ is an attribute of ʿAd, Thamud and Pharaoh, and it may be in the accusative as a formula of blame, or the predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾: the scourge is used as a metaphor for punishment, because it entails repetition that the sword and other weapons do not entail. This was said by Ibn ʿAtiyya. **Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 89, verses 15–16:**

﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him﴾. The *ibtila'* (trial) is *al-ikhtibar* (testing), and God's testing of His servant is so that the proof (*hujja*) is established against the servant by what appears from him. God had known this before it occurred. Here "man" (*al-insan*) refers to the category of humankind. It has been said that the verse was revealed concerning Utba ibn Rabi'a, but it is nonetheless general, applying to whoever has this characteristic.

God mentions in this verse His testing of man with ease (*al-khayr*), and then mentions His testing of him with hardship (*al-sharr*), as He said in al-Anbiya' [35]: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good﴾. He also rebukes him for his saying when given ease, "My Lord has honoured me," and his saying when given hardship, "My Lord has humiliated me." Two questions arise concerning the verse:

**The first question:** Why did God rebuke man for saying "My Lord has honoured me" and "My Lord has humiliated me"? The answer has two aspects. First, man says "My Lord has honoured me" out of boastfulness and pride, not out of gratitude. And he says "My Lord has humiliated me" out of complaint against God, lack of patience, and failure to submit to God's decree. So God rebukes him for what his words imply, since it is obligatory for him to be grateful for ease and patient in hardship. Second, man takes the world as the measure: he considers the expansion of provision in it to be honour, and its restriction to be humiliation, but the matter is not so. God may expand provision for His enemies and restrict it for His friends. So God rebukes him for measuring by the world and for heedlessness of the Hereafter. This rebuke, in this respect, applies to the believer. As for the disbeliever, he measures by the world because he does not affirm the Hereafter and regards the world as the ultimate end, so God rebukes him for what his words imply.

**The second question:** If it is said, God has said ﴿then He honours him﴾, affirming his honour, how then does He rebuke him for saying "My Lord has honoured me"? The answer is in three aspects. First, He did not rebuke him for mentioning the honour, but rebuked him for what his words indicate of boastfulness and lack of gratitude, or of measuring by the world rather than the Hereafter, as we have mentioned regarding the meaning of the rebuke. Second, He rebukes him for saying "My Lord has honoured me" if he believes that God's honouring him is due to his deserving honour, as a matter of merit and favour, like the saying of Qarun: ﴿It was given to me only because of knowledge I have﴾ [al-Qasas: 78]. Third, the rebuke is only for his saying "My Lord has humiliated me," not for his saying "My Lord has honoured me," since "My Lord has honoured me" is an acknowledgement of God's blessing, whereas "My Lord has humiliated me" is a complaint about God's action.

﴿So He restricted his provision﴾, meaning He narrowed it for him. It is recited with the *dal* doubled (*tashdid*) and with it single (*takhfif*), with the same meaning. The doubling carries added emphasis. It has also been said that the meaning of the doubled form is that He made it according to a known measure.

﴿Kallā﴾ (Nay/No indeed), a rebuke against what he denied of the words of man. ﴿Bal lā tukrimūna al-yatīm﴾ (Rather, you do not honour the orphan). This is a censure of the ugly deeds mentioned. The meaning of this "bal" (rather) as a turning away (idrāb) is as if He denied on man what preceded, then said: "Rather, you do what is worse than that, which is that you do not honour the orphan, and what is mentioned after it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The dearest of houses to Allah is a house in which there is an orphan who is honoured."

﴿Wa-lā taḥāḍḍūna ʿalā ṭaʿām al-miskīn﴾ (And you do not urge one another to feed the poor). Ḥaḍḍ upon a matter (al-ḥaḍḍ ʿalā al-amr) is encouragement toward it, and whoever does not urge others to a matter does not do it himself. It is as if this is a censure of abandoning the feeding of the poor. Here ṭaʿām means ikhrām (feeding/giving food). It was also said that it is elided with a omitted modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf), its meaning being: "You do not urge one another to give the food of the poor." It was read as tuḥāḍḍūna with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ and an alif after it, meaning: "None of you urges another."

﴿Wa-taʾkulūna al-turāth akllan lammā﴾ (And you devour the inheritance, devouring all together). Al-turāth is the wealth that is inherited from the deceased, and the tāʾ in it is a substitution for the wāw. Al-lamm means gathering and collecting. The construction is: "devouring that which is gathered," which is that one takes in the inheritance his share and the share of others, because the Arabs did not give a female or a young child any of the inheritance; rather, it was reserved for the men.

﴿Wa-tuḥibbūna al-māla ḥubbān jammā﴾ (And you love wealth with an abundant love). That is, intensely and greatly. This is a censure of greed for wealth and of intense desire for it.

It was also said that it is elided with a omitted modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf), its meaning being: "You do not urge one another to give the food of the poor." It was read as tuḥāḍḍūna with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ and an alif after it, meaning: "None of you urges another."

﴿Wa-taʾkulūna al-turāth akllan lammā﴾ (And you devour the inheritance, devouring all together). Al-turāth is the wealth that is inherited from the deceased, and the tāʾ in it is a substitution for the wāw. Al-lamm means gathering and collecting. The construction is: "devouring that which is gathered," which is that one takes in the inheritance his share and the share of others, because the Arabs did not give a female or a young child any of the inheritance; rather, it was reserved for the men.

﴿Wa-tuḥibbūna al-māla ḥubbān jammā﴾ (And you love wealth with an abundant love). That is, intensely and greatly. This is a censure of greed for wealth and of intense desire for it.

﴿The earth is pounded to powder﴾, meaning its mountains are leveled. ﴿Pounded, pounded﴾, meaning pounded again and again, as you say, "I learned the knowledge door by door." ﴿And your Lord comes﴾. Its interpretation (ta'wil) according to those who interpret it is: His command and His authority come. Al-Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: its meaning is His manifestation to the creation at that time. This verse and similar ones are among the ambiguous matters (mushkilat) in which one must believe without specifying the modality (takyif) or likening (tamthil). ﴿And the angels﴾: "al-malak" here is a collective noun, as it is related that all the angels will be arranged in rows around the earth. ﴿Row upon row﴾, meaning one row after another, having encircled the jinn and mankind. ﴿And Hell will be brought forth on that Day﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hell will be brought on that Day with seventy thousand bridles, and with each bridle seventy thousand angels pulling it."

﴿On that Day, man will remember﴾. "Yawma'idhin" is a substitute (badal) for "idha dukkati" (when the earth is pounded), and "yatadhakkaru" (will remember) is its governing verb (al-'amil), and it is the response (jawab) of "idha dukkati". The meaning is that man will remember on the Day of Resurrection his deeds in this world, and will regret his neglect and disobedience. "Al-insan" (man) here is generic. It is also said that it refers to 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, and it is said that it refers to Umayya ibn Khalaf. ﴿And how will the remembrance benefit him?﴾ This is elliptical, its implied meaning being: how can he benefit from the remembrance? Just as you say, "He regretted when regret did not benefit him." ﴿He will say: "Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life﴾. There are two interpretations of this: first, that he means the life of the Hereafter, so the meaning is: "Oh, I wish I had sent forth righteous deeds for the Hereafter." Second, that he means the life of this world, so the meaning is: "Oh, I wish I had sent forth righteous deeds during my life." In this case, the "li" (for) is like the statement "I wrote it for ten days of the month" (li-'ashr min al-shahr). ﴿So on that Day, none will punish as He punishes, nor will anyone bind as He binds﴾. Whoever reads "yu'adhdhibu" with a kasra on the dhal and "yuthiqu" with a kasra on the tha', then the pronoun in "'adhabahu" (His punishment) and "wathaqahu" (His binding) refers to Allah, Exalted, and the meaning is that Allah Himself undertakes the punishment of the disbelievers and does not entrust it to anyone. Whoever reads with a fatha, then the pronoun refers to man, meaning: no one punishes with a punishment like his, and no one binds with a binding like his. This is the reading of al-Kisa'i, and it is related that Abu 'Amr returned to it. It is a good reading, and it has been related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿O soul at peace﴾, that is, the one certain in its certainty, at rest in it, such that no doubt in faith can reach it. It was also said: "the soul at peace" is the one that feels no fear at that time. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: ﴿O soul at peace﴾ ﴿Return to your Lord﴾. This address and call occur at the time of death. It was also said: at the time of resurrection, and it was said: at the time when people depart to Paradise or the Fire. The first is more preferred, because it is narrated that Abu Bakr asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about this, and he said to him: "O Abu Bakr, the angel will say it to you at your death."

﴿Well-pleased﴾: its meaning is pleased with what He has given it, or pleased with Allah. And the meaning of ﴿well-pleasing﴾ is one who is pleasing in the sight of Allah, or Allah has made it pleased by what He has given it. ﴿So enter among My servants﴾, that is, enter into the company of My righteous servants. It was read as "fa-adkhuli fi 'abdi" (in the singular), meaning "enter into his body," and this is an address to the soul. This verse was revealed concerning Hamzah. It was also said: concerning Khubayb ibn 'Adi, whom the disbelievers crucified in Makkah. Its wording, however, is general and includes every soul at peace.
